notes: Point first to the bottom-left quadrant: the problem is not whether women work, but whether the system recognizes that work economically. Emphasize that this slide adds a gender-execution lens to the water, productivity, and value-chain story already shown.
title: Women’s agricultural work remains economically undercounted, which suppresses adoption, enterprise participation, and resilience in Gujarat’s farm households
subtitle: The constraint is not labor presence but weak recognition in land, credit, extension, and market systems, which blocks women from converting work into decisions and income.

children.title: Women contribute heavily to farm work, but **asset, service, and market recognition** still sits below their economic role
children.subtitle: When labor is visible but control over inputs, training, finance, and sales remains limited, productivity and resilience gains leak out at household level

rows: Time burden from care and water collection

content.text: Recognition gaps weaken exactly the levers Gujarat now needs most: faster *micro-irrigation* uptake, more disciplined crop management, stronger aggregation, and participation in higher-value chains such as dairy, horticulture, and processing.

rows: Women work fields but often do not choose crops
Climate response depends on fast practice change
Households adopt slower when key workers are missed
Value capture needs grading and enterprise roles
Women’s labor stays unpaid or low-paid
Shock resilience depends on diversified earnings
Less control reduces fallback income options

children.takeaway: The intervention logic is clear: move women from invisible contributors toward enabled producers by tying extension, finance, irrigation, and market access to the people already doing the work.

footnote: Source: FAO, World Bank, IFPRI, Government of India agriculture and gender literature, and National Family Health Survey reference findings [[src:official]]
